name: Paluan
confidence_why: No source states where Paluan word stress falls: Prentice 1971 (the same fieldwork as his 1969 thesis) gives penultimate stress only for Timugon and says nothing about stress in his Paluan outline, which by his own rule reports only features that differ from Timugon, Rutter 1929 merely assumes penultimate accent "as in Malay" across thirteen wordlists at once, and Lobel 2013 and Spitzack 1984 are silent, so a penultimate reading for Paluan is an inference rather than a finding.

catalog_quote: [p.274, 10.0] The descriptions are of necessity based on the detailed analysis of the Poros subdialect of Timugon already presented ... The same terminology is used in the outline studies as was used in the Timugon grammar and attention is focused mainly on those features which exhibit differences with Timugon. ... The next section gives an account of the phonology, including an inventory of phonemes and a description of any distributional or allophonic features which differ significantly from the Timugon pattern. [p.287, 10.3.1.1 Phonology] The phoneme inventory of the Paluan subdialect is /p t k ʔ b d g m n ŋ s l y w i u o a/, which, except for the absence of /j/, is identical with that of Timugon. The Dalit and Sapulut subdialects, however, do have a /j/ phoneme. No evidence was found of the existence of a phoneme /*ñ/. All three subdialects differ, both from each other and from the Lowland Murut dialects, in their realisation of the phonemes /b d g/ ... [p.14, 2.2.1 STRESS, Timugon] Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. ... 2.2.1.1 Strong stress. Strong stress (marked by ´) occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2): /mamatoy/ [...] 'will kill' /potoyon/ [...] 'will be killed'

Book page = PDF page - 12. (1) p.14 = p.26, sec. 2.2.1 Stress: 'Stress appears to be non-phonemic in Timugon, as its occurrence is always, with very few exceptions (see 2.3.3.3), predictable from the word- and phrase-structure. No minimal pairs have been found in which differences in stress are not accompanied by phonemic differences' and 2.2.1.1 'Strong stress (marked by ') occurs on the penultimate syllable of the word (see also 2.3.4.1.2): /mamatoy/.. /potoyon/'; 2.2.1.2 weak stress on the first syllable when separated from s…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary (strong) stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the word and is non-contrastive; this is stated explicitly for Timugon Murut, and Prentice's first-hand outline of Paluan, which by his stated convention records only departures from the Timugon pattern, reports no stress difference, so Paluan is described (implicitly) as sharing penultimate stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: For Timugon (and by extension the outlines): a weak stress falls on the first syllable of the word when it is separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables; weak stress also replaces strong stress on a word subordinate to another within a phrase (p.14).
new_statements.exceptions: Timugon 2.3.3.3.1 (p.24): a few words, particularly those ending in -aCa?, are stressed on the last syllable (kaga?, madada?, masaga?); long (type-1 cluster) penultimate vowels carry the stress; in rising diphthongs stress shifts to the second vowel, and in some -ia/-io words to the antepenult (pp.24-25). None of these are restated for Paluan.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level strong stress; the phrase is defined as containing a single strong stress, with word stress demoted to weak stress on phrase-subordinate words (p.13-14). Explicit rule is for the Poros subdialect of Timugon; application to Paluan rests on the differences-only framing of ch.10, not on a Paluan-specific sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: The explicit stress rule (non-phonemic, strong stress on the penult) is stated for Timugon Murut, Poros subdialect (timu1245), in Prentice 1971 ch.2. Paluan (palu1253; Prentice's 'Paluan dialect of Highland Murut', subdialects Paluan proper, Dalit, Sapulut; informant K.K. Ampatang bin Inggu of Dalit Tengah) is covered first-hand in the ch.10 outline, which by the author's stated convention (p.274) records only phonological features differing from Timugon and reports none for stress. Any catalog entry should be tiered as 'penult, inferred from a differences-only outline', not as a Paluan-specific sentence. Spitzack 1984 treats 'Paluan language' = Paluan dialect + Pandewan Murut.

new_statements.relation_note: This is the thesis text of the existing statement's source (Prentice 1971, Pacific Linguistics C-18): same chapter and section numbering, different pagination (thesis p.23 = book p.14; thesis p.458 = book p.274; Paluan phonology thesis p.481 = book p.287). Same placement (penultimate, non-phonemic), same secondary-stress and exception detail, same differences-only convention for the Paluan outline. Adds nothing new for Paluan; confirms that no outline study in ch.10 reports a stress difference for Paluan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-phonemic and predictable: strong stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. Stated directly for the Timugon dialect of Lowland Murut (Poros subdialect); for Paluan the thesis's outline (10.3.1.1, pp.481-483) lists only the phoneme inventory and /b d g/ allophony under the chapter-10 convention of reporting only features that differ from Timugon, so the penultimate rule is inferred for Paluan, not stated in a Paluan-specific sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Weak stress (2.2.1.2, p.23, Timugon): (1) on the first syllable of the word when it is separated from the strong stress by two or more syllables, e.g. /pamamagambad/ 'camera'; (2) weak stress replaces strong stress in a word subordinate to another within a phrase (one strong stress per phrase, 2.1 p.22).
new_statements.exceptions: 2.3.3.3.1 Irregular stress (p.32): 'A few words, particularly those ending in /-aCaʔ/, are stressed on the last syllable: /kagaʔ/ "very", /madadaʔ/ "dislike", and /masagaʔ/ "wish"'. 2.3.4.1.2 (pp.35-36): vowel clusters shift stress (type 2 rising diphthongs carry stress on the second vowel; word-final /-io/ clusters carry word stress on the antepenult, e.g. /ginio/, /lumbio/; type 3 falling diphthongs transfer stress to the first member). Sumambuq remark p.491: Lees's analysis 'fails to account for the stress difference in such pairs as /kadui/ "porcupine" and /kanuy/ "eagle"'. All of these are Timugon (or Sumambuq) facts; nothing Paluan-specific.
new_statements.identity_note: The stress rule is stated for the Timugon dialect of Lowland Murut, Poros subdialect (Glottolog timu1262 Timugon Murut), not for Paluan. Prentice's 'Paluan' (thesis sec. 10.3.1, pp.480-488) is a dialect of the Highland Murut language with three subdialects: Paluan proper (representative; informant K.K. Ampatang bin Inggu of Dalit Tengah, headman of Barong; Punti, Dalit and Keramatoi headwaters, Padas valley Kemabong-Segah, Pangi river), Dalit (Sook plain; informant Sgt Joseph Marantai) and Sapulut (Talankai river; informant Kunsi bin Buau). Prentice notes (p.478) that the term 'Paluan' is extended to speech-forms whose speakers would not use it, and that 'Tagol', 'Sumambuq' and 'Pensiangan Murut' are used indiscriminately for Highland Murut speakers; the 1964 English-Murut Phrase Book informant was a Dalit-subdialect Paluan speaker.
